L	In my childhood, fire had two faces. The first: friendly, vivacious, exuberant. Like a puppy
with sharp teeth and too much energy, capable of doing damage but not out of malicious
intent. Fire as community, as celebration, as connection. Beach bonfires made of sand-crusted
driftwood, pulsing an unpredictable pattern of light and heat into the starry night, sending
glimmers off the black lake. Pine-scented fires made from dried-out Christmas trees, around
which my cousins and aunts and uncles and friends huddled, the flames sometimes erupting
blue as a forgotten strand of tinsel burned up, nearby ice hissing as it melted. Campfires to
cook hot dogs, roast vegetables wrapped in foil or toast marshmallows to the perfect shade of
golden brown. Simmering prairie burns that leave the earth blackened, amplifying the sun-fed
warmth to spring plants, smelling like sweet charcoal. I loved all the fires, always volunteered
to get them started, wanted nothing more than to sit and watch the ripple and dance of flame
till there was nothing but snapping embers.
The second: deadly, unpredictable, bad to know. House fires that killed sleeping children or
leveled historic cities. Grease fires in the kitchen, subverting the normal knowledge of
quenching them with water. Frayed wires allowing electrons to escape their confines and
ignite furniture. Stop, drop and roll; in emergencies break glass; test the smoke detector on a
regular basis. If that alarm goes off, feel the doorknob before opening your bedroom door.
Block smoke with a towel. Open the window, hang from the ledge and drop if you have no
other option; better to break an ankle than burn to death or die of smoke inhalation. Fire has
no place indoors, except on carefully monitored candles, and the friendliness of a bonfire
should not be mistaken for house-training.
Wildfires belong to this second category as well, but on a far more massive scale. They were
also, notably, not a threat to my particular corner of North America; the Chicago fire of 1871
was old history by the time I moved there, even if it is represented on the city’s flag in the
form of a star. We had heat waves and polar vortexes, blizzards and tornadoes, floods and
droughts. I took comfort in the knowledge that fire happened in different ecological regimes.

Ill.	At a moment when the world once again teeters on the edge of catastrophic conflict, I find
myself returning to the memory of another time in the 1960s, when dissent was not only
possible but transformative. Today, as war rhetoric escalates, and the language of power
grows increasingly unrestrained, I am struck by the absence of a comparable collective moral
force.
I came of age in the mid-1960s, entering my undergraduate years at a time when the world
seemed alive with argument, possibility, and resistance. Unlike the present, the university
was a space charged with debate and intellectual exchange. We did not simply inherit the
world, we interrogated it.
But just as formative as the university were the informal spaces we inhabited. The coffeehouse
culture of those years, the dimly lit rooms filled with cigarette smoke, the clattering cups, and
restless voices, became an extension of intellectual life. It was there that ideas found their
urgency. Conversations moved from literature to politics, from philosophy to the daily
headlines of war and protest. Democracy, freedom, human rights far from being abstract
concepts, were debated intensely, often passionately.
Music, theatre, and radical thought became some of the most powerful carriers of this spirit of
interrogation. Sitting with friends, often late into the night, we read the incendiary writings of
Jean-Paul Sartre and Herbert Marcuse, whose critiques of consumer capitalism and
conformity unsettled our certainties. Their insistence that modern societies could produce not
freedom but new forms of domination forced us to rethink the very meaning of democracy. At
the same time, the political courage of figures like Martin Luther King Jr., with his
uncompromising stand against racial injustice, and Malcolm X, with his fierce articulation of
dignity and resistance, expanded our sense of what dissent could achieve. These were not
distant figures; they were intellectual and moral presences that shaped our conversations,

IV.	A US jury on Wednesday found Meta and YouTube guilty of deliberately designing addictive
products that caused harm to a young user in a landmark social media addiction trial that will
likely serve as a bellwether for future cases. The jurors in a Los Angeles court found the tech
companies to be negligent in the design of the platform and in failing to warn users of its
dangers. The jury said yes to questions that asked whether the platforms acted with malice,
oppression and fraud. The jury awarded damages of $6 million, with Meta bearing around 70%
of the liability and YouTube the remaining 30%.
Meta owns Facebook and Instagram and has over 3.5 billion users, while nine out of ten
American teenagers aged 13-17 overwhelmingly use YouTube, according to a 2025 Pew
Research Center report. Meta has long been accused of addictive platform design by parents,
child safety groups and tech policy advocates, and of causing mental health issues resulting in
eating disorders and self-harm. The present case is the first in a flurry of lawsuits filed by
teenagers, school districts and states, claiming that platforms like Meta-owned Instagram and
‘YouTube were designed to encourage excessive use by millions of young Americans. Twenty-
year-old KGM started using YouTube when she was six, and Instagram at nine. She claimed
that her addiction to social media led to anxiety, depression and body dysmorphia. The
plaintiffs have argued that social media should be identified as a product and thus its design
and other components must be held to product liability standards.
Mark Lanier, her lawyer, compared this design to dopamine-seeking “slot machines”, and said
that YouTube and Meta were operating like “digital casinos” with their endless scroll features
fuelling dopamine hits and thus, addiction. Past lawsuits against social media companies over
the harm they cause frequently ran into Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act 1996,
which says that internet platforms cannot be held liable for content posted by their users.
Courts had read it broadly enough to kill most lawsuits before they got anywhere near a jury.
The plaintiffs in this case avoided that barrier by changing the claim itself, framing it instead
around product design. It thus drew on principles from product liability law, where liability
can arise from how a product is built rather than what it contains. [Word Count: 319]

XI.	An agreement is a mutual understanding or arrangement between two or more parties. It
represents the meeting of minds where each party agrees to do or not do something.
Agreements can be oral, written, formal, informal, or implied by conduct. Section 2(e) of the
Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines an agreement as “every promise and every set of promises,
forming the consideration for each other.” In simple terms, when one person makes an offer
and the other accepts it, it becomes an agreement. Agreements are flexible in nature and may
be verbal, written, or implied by actions. However, not all agreements are enforceable by law.
For example, a verbal promise between friends to meet, an informal arrangement to share
expenses, or an email exchange regarding meeting details may be agreements, but they may
not create legal consequences.
A contract, on the other hand, is a legally binding agreement that the law recognises and
enforces. Section 2(h) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 defines a contract as “an agreement
enforceable by law.” A contract creates legal rights and obligations between the parties. If one
party fails to perform their part, the other party may seek legal remedies such as
compensation, specific performance, or cancellation. Examples of contracts include
employment contracts, lease agreements, sale deeds, service agreements and loan agreements.
Thus, every contract is an agreement, but every agreement is not a contract.
For an agreement to become a contract, it must satisfy certain essential elements. There must
be a lawful offer by one party and an unequivocal acceptance by the other. There must be
lawful consideration, meaning something of value such as money, goods, services, or a promise
to do or not do something. The parties must be competent to contract, meaning they must be
major, of sound mind, and not disqualified by law. Their consent must be free and genuine, not
caused by coercion, undue influence, fraud, misrepresentation or mistake. The object must be
lawful, and the terms must be certain and capable of performance. If any of these essential
elements are absent, the agreement remains unenforceable.www.lawpreptutorial.com

XII. Peaceful settlement of disputes in international law, also known as pacific settlement of
international disputes, is a fundamental principle requiring States to resolve their
disagreements by peaceful means so that international peace, security and justice are not
endangered. Its origin can be traced to the Hague Peace Conferences of 1899 and 1907, which
produced conventions for the pacific settlement of disputes. The principle gained greater
importance after the prohibition on the use of force under Article 2(4) of the UN Charter.
Article 2(3) of the UN Charter provides that all members shall settle their international
disputes by peaceful means. This obligation was reaffirmed in the 1982 Manila Declaration on
the Peaceful Settlement of International Disputes.
An international dispute may be understood as a disagreement involving at least one State
and another State, international organisation, natural person, legal person, institution or
corporation from another part of the world. The Black’s Law Dictionary defines a dispute as a
conflict or controversy, especially one giving rise to legal proceedings. In international law,
peaceful settlement is treated as a continuous legal duty, where States participate as equal
units in rights. In Military and Paramilitary Activities in and against Nicaragua, the ICJ
recognised that parties to a dispute must seek a solution by pacific methods. However, the UN
Charter does not compel parties to adopt one fixed method. Article 33 lists peaceful methods
such as negotiation, enquiry, mediation, conciliation, arbitration, judicial settlement and
resort to regional arrangements. If parties fail to settle the dispute, Article 37 requires them to
refer the matter to the Security Council.
Negotiation is the oldest, simplest and most common method. It involves direct discussion
between disputing parties without third-party intervention. India and Sri Lanka settled their
boundary dispute through negotiation in 1974, and the Farakka Barrage issue between India
and Bangladesh was also resolved through this method. Good offices involve a third friendly
State, individual or organisation suggesting settlement without directly participating in
discussions, as seen in the Shatt-al-Arab dispute between Iran and Iraq through the President
of Algeria. Mediation involves active participation of a neutral third party who gives
suggestions and helps parties reach settlement; the Tashkent Agreement between India and
Pakistan is an example.
Conciliation refers disputes to a commission or committee which proposes a settlement,
though its recommendations are not binding. Arbitration and judicial settlement are
adjudicative methods because they result in binding decisions. Arbitration involves a chosen
arbitrator or tribunal, while judicial settlement involves courts such as the International
Court of Justice. International disputes may be legal or political, but international law mainly
deals with legal disputes. In Nicaragua v. Honduras, the Court clarified that it concerns itself
only with legal aspects of a dispute. [Word Count: 449]

XIII. Bailable offences are those offences where the accused has a legal right to be released on bail.
Under BNSS, such offences are specifically marked as bailable in the First Schedule. These
offences are generally treated as less serious, and therefore the accused is not required to
remain in custody till the court conducts an elaborate hearing. The primary feature of a
bailable offence is that the police officer in charge can release the accused on bail after arrest
once the required bond is furnished. There is no need to wait for a court order or a complex
hearing at this stage. These offences usually involve minor harm, limited property loss,
personal disputes, or conduct having low impact on public safety.
The classification of some offences as bailable is based on the idea that unnecessary detention
should be avoided where the alleged act does not involve grave injury, severe consequences,
major threat to public order, or serious social harm. Common examples include simple hurt,
minor trespass, rash or negligent driving, obstruction in public pathways, defamation,
criminal intimidation, minor cheating, mischief causing small loss, falsification of accounts,
negligent acts likely to spread infection, and misconduct in public by intoxicated persons.
Although bailable offences are generally minor, an offence with higher punishment may
sometimes still be classified as bailable due to legislative intent or specific policy
considerations.
Non-bailable offences are more serious offences where the accused does not have a right to
bail. Release from custody depends on the discretion of the court. These offences often involve
serious violence, sexual offences, crimes against children, repeated criminal conduct, major
financial fraud, threat to national security, or significant danger to public order. In such cases,
the court examines the gravity of allegations, the nature of evidence, possibility of the accused
fleeing, past criminal record, risk of influencing witnesses, impact on society or victim, and the
need for proper investigation before granting bail.
The major difference between bailable and non-bailable offences lies in the right to bail and
the authority granting it. In bailable offences, bail is available as a matter of right and may be
granted by the police officer or the court. In non-bailable offences, bail is not a right and only

XIV. In tort law, when a wrongful act is committed by more than one person, the persons involved
may be joint tortfeasors or independent tortfeasors. Joint tortfeasors are those who act
together or in furtherance of a common design, resulting in damage to another person. Their
liability is joint and several, which means that each tortfeasor is individually liable for the
entire damage and also collectively liable with the others. Independent tortfeasors, on the
other hand, act separately and without coordination. Even if their separate acts cause the
same injury, their liability arises from separate causes of action. In The Koursk, it was
observed that joint liability requires concerted action towards a common end, and mere
similarity of conduct is not enough.
The difference between independent and joint tortfeasors is important for determining
remedies. In Thompson v. London County Council, damage occurred due to separate negligent
acts of different parties, and the Court held that they were not joint tortfeasors because their
acts were independent. Similarly, in The Koursk, two ships were treated as independent
tortfeasors because there was no common design. Joint liability may arise in cases of agency,
vicarious liability, or common action. Under agency, if one person authorises another to act on
his behalf, both may be liable for torts committed within that authority. Vicarious liability
arises from relationships such as employer and employee, where one person is made liable for
the wrongful act of another. Joint liability also arises where two or more persons act together,
assist, or instigate a tort.www.lawpreptutorial.com

sue all tortfeasors together, sue any one of them individually, or recover the entire

the whole damage caused.

XVI. Over the past few weeks, the sharp slide in the rupee’s exchange rate has stroked a long-
pending debate about the true state of the Indian economy. Be that as it may, the urgent
policy decision before the government and the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is whether to
prevent the rupee from further sliding against the US dollar or to let it fall and find its true
level.
For the uninitiated, the rupee’s exchange rate against the US dollar basically changes
depending on the relative demand for the two currencies in the foreign exchange (forex)
markets. If Indians demand more dollars (either to buy foreign goods or to invest in other
countries) than the rupees demanded by foreigners (either to buy Indian goods or to invest in
India) then the relative value (exchange rate) moves in favour of the dollar; that is, rupee’s
exchange rate worsens, as indeed it has done in the recent past. If foreigners demand more
rupees than Indians demand dollars, then the rupee’s exchange rate improves. It goes without
saying then that the worsening of the rupee’s exchange rate is reflective of a weakness of the
Indian economy relative to the rest of the world. Seen from this lens, it makes sense to focus
on bolstering the domestic economy instead of wasting time trying to artificially improve the
rupee’s exchange rate.
Indians can’t hold dollars with them for regular use within the country. As such, even if they
get the dollars on their way back from foreign visits, all dollars flow back to the RBI. This
stash of dollars with the RBI can be employed by the central bank to artificially boost the
rupee’s exchange rate when needed.
Imagine a scenario where US investors decide to pull out billions of dollars from their Indian
investments with a view to either investing the money back in US firms or in firms of some
other countries, say, South Korea. Suppose they sell their stake in Indian companies, take the
rupees they got as a result to the forex market to get dollars; after all they need dollars to
transact outside India. This creates a sudden increase in the supply of rupees (without any
new demand for those rupees) and an increase in the demand for dollars (without any new
supply for dollars). The only way to resolve this situation is if the rupee weakens against the
dollar — in other words, if every additional dollar can be bought by exchanging more rupees
than before.
